summary: Gives a methodology for benchmarking local area network (LAN) switching devices. It describes how to run tests so results can be compared. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2889 describes repeatable tests for LAN switches, including how much traffic they forward, whether they lose frames, and how they learn addresses. It also specifies how to report test conditions so readers can interpret results.

questions: how do you benchmark a lan switch
subtitle: A repeatable method for measuring how LAN switches forward frames and handle load.

tldr.problem: Switch performance tests need consistent setups and reporting so results from different devices can be compared.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2889 defines test traffic patterns, setup checks, measurements and reporting for frame forwarding, congestion, address handling, filtering and broadcast traffic.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo extends the general benchmarking method in RFC 2544 to LAN switching devices. Its results depend on following the stated procedures and reporting the offered load and frame conditions.

today: RFC 2889 is an Informational memo published in August 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Test Requirements
sections.content:
This memo extends RFC 2544 benchmarking to LAN devices that switch frames at the Media Access Control (MAC) layer. It covers forwarding performance, congestion control, latency, address handling and filtering, and gives formats for reporting results.

It adopts the benchmark-test template from RFC 2544 and uses the requirement words defined in RFC 2119. Before each run, the device under test (DUT) MUST learn the test MAC addresses; otherwise it may flood frames and distort the results.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives procedures for comparing LAN switches. Before each test, the switch must learn the addresses used in the test so unknown addresses do not cause extra frame flooding.

sections.title: Prepare the Device and Test Frames
sections.content:
Testers should verify address learning and set the address-aging time long enough that learned entries remain during the trial. A switch that uses hashing may not learn every chosen address, so the test frame format must allow addresses to be rearranged.

Test frames need a unique signature in their UDP data area so the tester can distinguish them from frames generated by the device or misforwarded by it. The memo describes standard Ethernet frames and tagged forms. Tagged frames may exceed the standard 1518-byte maximum and may not work with every device.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep learned addresses from expiring during a test and mark test frames so they can be counted accurately. Check that the switch accepts the frame type and size being tested.

sections.title: The Benchmark Tests
sections.content:
The memo defines ten tests. Traffic tests include fully meshed forwarding, one-to-many and many-to-one traffic, multiple devices with a backbone link, and unidirectional traffic. Other tests examine congestion control, forward pressure, address-table capacity, address-learning rate, error filtering, and broadcast forwarding and latency.

For meshed traffic, ports send to destinations in a round-robin pattern so the offered load is balanced. In a congestion test, some traffic is sent to an uncongested port while other traffic overloads a congested port; frame loss at the uncongested port can indicate head-of-line blocking.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests cover traffic across many ports, congestion, forwarding limits, address-table behavior, bad frames and broadcasts. The traffic pattern matters because an unbalanced test can produce inconsistent results.

sections.title: Measurements and Reporting
sections.content:
Throughput is the maximum offered load at which the device has zero frame loss. Forwarding rate counts test frames successfully sent to the correct destination per second at a stated offered load. Maximum forwarding rate is the highest forwarding rate found by adjusting the input load.

Frame-loss measurements should be taken at the end of the trial. The recommended frame sizes are 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280 and 1518 bytes, and the recommended trial duration is 30 seconds. Results should identify test parameters and are often shown in graphs comparing theoretical and measured results.
sections.plainLanguage: Report how many frames arrived correctly, how many were lost, and the offered load used. Include frame size and trial conditions so another reader can understand the result.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The memo says it describes test metrics, not a protocol or protocol implementation, and therefore has no security considerations associated with it.

RFC 2889 is an Informational benchmarking methodology. It measures device behavior; it does not specify switch features or guarantee a particular performance result.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a test methodology, not a network protocol. It does not make a switch meet a particular performance target.

items.title: Throughput
items.text: Maximum offered load with zero frame loss.

items.title: Forwarding rate
items.text: Correctly forwarded test frames per second at a stated load.

items.title: Frame loss
items.text: Frames that do not reach the correct destination.

items.title: Address capacity
items.text: The number of addresses the device can learn without flooding.
